title: The First Hundred
_comment: startDate anchors the pack to the calendar. Every install computes today's day number from this date, so everyone on this build sees the same prompt on the same day without a server. Changing it reshuffles which prompt lands on which date for everybody.
_sequence: Ordered by skill, not by subject: line and shape (1-14), proportion (15-26), form and ellipses (27-40), perspective (41-54), value (55-66), texture (67-76), organic and gesture (77-87), faces (88-96), composition (97-100). 'focus' names the one thing to practise and, on the harder days, deliberately shrinks the task — scope creep is what makes people quit around day 60.

prompts.focus: One continuous outline. Try not to lift the pencil.
Draw the centre vein first, then hang the outline off it.
Straight lines only. Keep the shaft one clean stroke.
Two mirrored curves. Check the halves actually match.
Four straight edges and a flap. Watch the angles.
Light strokes outward from the shaft. Vary the pressure.
Only the folds. Five or six lines should do it.
Two shapes joined by a bridge. Keep them the same size.
Flat front only, no depth yet. Sharp corners.
A long taper. Keep both edges parallel until the point.
A soft square, a string, a tag. Nothing else.
Space the tines evenly. That is the whole exercise.
Two crossing shapes. Get the crossing point right.
A symmetry test. Fold it in half in your head.
Measure height against width before you commit.
Bowl or stem — which is taller? Check, do not guess.
Glass to base ratio. Most people draw the base too small.
Body against shackle. Compare the two.
Brim width against crown height.
The handles are shorter than you think. Measure them.
Two feet, two bells, one face. Keep them even.
Line the spout tip up with the lid. It usually matches.
Compare the spout length to the body width.
Sole to ankle ratio. Draw the sole line first.
Straps are about half the body width. Check first.
The upper bout is smaller than the lower. Prove it.
An ellipse top and bottom. The lower one is rounder.
A cylinder. The rim is an ellipse, not a line.
Two ellipses sharing one centre line.
Keep the ellipse square to the jar's axis.
A dome over a cylinder. Find where the two meet.
No straight lines anywhere. One end is wider.
A spiral turning in space, not a flat one.
The shell is the exercise. The body is a bonus.
A box and a dome stacked. Keep the axis vertical.
The shoulder is the hard part. Curve it in three dimensions.
A circle seen at an angle is an ellipse. Commit to it.
Three spheres sitting inside one wider ellipse.
Nested cylinders. Each ellipse rounds out as it turns away.
Just the horn. A cone, and its mouth is one big ellipse.
Two planes meeting. The far page is shorter.
Three faces, one vanishing point. No edge stays parallel.
Back legs are shorter on the page. Trust that.
Every horizontal points at the same place. Find it first.
Look through it. The frame is a box, not a rectangle.
Draw one step properly, then repeat it smaller.
The opening is a wedge, not a rectangle.
Everything sits on one flat plane. Establish it first.
Just the front wheel and forks. Get the ellipse right.
Looking up. The top reads smaller than the base.
Draw the two end slats, then divide the space between.
A long curved box. The far rim sits higher.
Repeating posts, each shorter and closer together.
Rows of keys stepping back. One row at a time.
One light source. The darkest point is not the edge.
Patches of light and dark. No outlines at all.
Draw what you see, not what you know. Mostly shapes of tone.
Reflections have hard edges. Almost nothing is mid-grey.
Light from below. Invert everything you assume.
Shade along the folds, never across them.
Three tones only. Light, mid, shadow. Resist a fourth.
The shadow matters more than the object throwing it.
Fill it solid. Shape carries the whole drawing.
Tone through distortion. Let the far things go soft.
Warm light from one point. Everything else falls away.
Two values. Resist adding a third.
Marks, not lines. Let the gaps do the work.
Get the weave right in one patch, imply the rest.
One patch of stitches in full. The rest is texture.
Ten bricks properly drawn. Suggest the hundred behind them.
Strokes follow the direction of growth. Nothing straight.
Overlapping layers, the largest at the bottom.
Broken edges and stains. Keep nothing smooth.
Spirals of scales. Start from the bottom row.
One twist, repeated along a curve.
Creased leather. The creases follow the foot inside.
One flowing line for the spine before anything else.
An egg and a circle. Gesture first, feathers never.
The tail carries the movement. Start there.
A single S curve. Everything else hangs off it.
Two boxes and a line. Angles, not curves.
Long lines, thin joints. Keep the legs light.
Symmetrical, but soften it. Nothing in nature is exact.
Eight rhythms, every one a different length.
The weight sits over the front legs. Show that.
Mass first. Draw the volume before a single wrinkle.
Every leaf points somewhere different. No two alike.
The eyeball is a sphere. The lids wrap around it.
Three planes. Find them before you draw an outline.
The upper lip is darker. Almost always.
Draw it as a spiral, not as a shape.
Block the palm as one shape before any fingers.
The eyes sit halfway down the head. Measure and see.
There is more skull behind the ear than you think.
The far eye is narrower. Commit to it.
Likeness comes from proportion, not from detail.
Choosing what to leave out is the exercise.
Lead the eye to one point. Everything else supports it.
Crowds are shapes. Only three figures get faces.
Everything you have learned. Take as long as you like.
